posts.title: Interest and APR are two views of the same cost.

slides.heading: Interest is the price of borrowing.
slides.body: When a balance carries past the due date, the card issuer charges interest on it. It is added to the balance, so next month there is a little more to charge interest on.

slides.heading: APR is the yearly rate.
slides.body: APR stands for annual percentage rate. A card at 24% APR charges about 2% a month. Statements show the APR; the interest line shows what that rate cost this month in dollars.

slides.heading: Cards charge daily, not monthly.
slides.body: Most issuers divide the APR by 365 and apply it to the balance every day. That is why paying a few days earlier saves a little, and why a balance grows faster than the yearly rate suggests.

slides.heading: Where to find it on a statement.
slides.body: Look for a box called "Interest Charge Calculation" or "APR." It lists purchase APR, cash advance APR, and any penalty APR. Penalty APRs are often above 29% and can apply after a late payment.

slides.heading: Why it matters.
slides.body: Two people can owe the same $5,000. At 12% APR the interest is about $50 a month at first. At 29% it is about $120. Same balance, very different cost.

posts.caption: Interest and APR describe the same thing from two angles: interest is the dollar cost of carrying a balance, APR is the yearly rate that produces it. Cards apply that rate daily, which is why balances grow faster than people expect and why a penalty APR after one late payment hurts so much. Knowing the APR on each account is the first step to any plan, because it tells you which balance is the most expensive to keep. If you want a clear picture of your own balances, the free review on our site takes about a minute. Link in bio.

posts.title: A $5,000 card paid at the minimum takes about 20 years to clear.

cover.title: A $5,000 card paid at the minimum takes about 20 years to clear.
cover.subtitle: Here is the math your statement is not showing you.

slides.heading: How the minimum is set
slides.body: Usually 1% of the balance plus that month's interest, or $25, whichever is more. On $5,000 at 24% APR, that is about $150 in month one.

slides.heading: Paying only the minimum
slides.label: in interest over about 20 years
slides.body: More than the original balance. The payment shrinks every month, so the account stays open as long as possible.

slides.heading: Same card. One habit changed.
slides.note: Keep the payment where it started and the interest drops to about $3,400.

slides.heading: Do this once
items: Find the payoff box on your statement
Pick a payment and never lower it
Set it to autopay
Watch the balance, not the minimum

posts.caption:
“Just pay the minimum” is the most expensive advice on your statement. 😬 $5,000 at 24% APR, minimums only: about 20 years and roughly $8,887 in interest. Keep the payment fixed at $150 and the same card is gone in about 5 years with about $3,400 in interest. Same debt, same rate, one habit. Swipe ➡️

posts.title: Your card charges interest every single day.

cover.title: Your card charges interest every single day.
cover.subtitle: Not once a month. Here is why that matters.

slides.heading: The daily rate
slides.label: per day at 24% APR
slides.body: Small on its own. But it applies every day to whatever is owed, and unpaid interest joins the balance.

slides.heading: Average daily balance
slides.body: Each day's balance is added up over the billing cycle and averaged. Interest is that average, times the daily rate, times the days in the cycle.

slides.heading: Timing is money
slides.body: A $2,000 payment on day 3 lowers the average for the whole month. The same payment on day 28 barely moves it. Earlier is cheaper.

slides.heading: The grace period rule
items: Pay the full statement balance by the due date: no interest on new purchases
Carry any balance: the grace period usually disappears
It comes back once the card is paid to zero

posts.caption:
Your card charges interest every day, not once a month. 📆 That changes two things: paying earlier in the billing cycle costs less than paying on the due date, and carrying any balance usually cancels your grace period on new purchases. Once you see the daily math, the statement stops being a mystery. Swipe ➡️

posts.title: Secured debt has collateral. Unsecured debt does not.

cover.title: Secured debt has collateral. Unsecured debt does not.
cover.subtitle: The first sort every plan starts with.

slides.heading: Secured
slides.body: A mortgage is backed by the house. An auto loan by the car. Stop paying and the lender can take the collateral. Rates are lower because of that safety net.

slides.heading: Unsecured
slides.body: Credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, store cards, collections. Nothing physical backs them. The lender's tools are interest, fees, collections, and sometimes a lawsuit.

slides.heading: Why it matters
items: Hardship programs, counseling plans, and settlement work with unsecured balances
Secured loans go through the lender, refinancing, or selling the asset
Federal student loans have their own rules

slides.heading: First step for any plan
slides.body: List every balance. Mark each one secured or unsecured. Most plans start by sorting the pile this way, because it shows which doors are open.

posts.caption:
Before any plan, sort the pile: secured or unsecured? 🗂️ Secured debt has collateral behind it (house, car). Unsecured debt does not (credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, collections). That one sort tells you which doors are open for each balance. Swipe ➡️

posts.title: Bankruptcy is not one thing. Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 work very differently.

cover.title: Bankruptcy is not one thing. Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 work very differently.
cover.subtitle: General information, not legal advice.

slides.heading: Chapter 7
slides.body: Often called liquidation. Non-exempt assets can be sold, and most remaining unsecured debt is discharged. Usually a few months. There is an income test to qualify.

slides.heading: Chapter 13
slides.body: A court-supervised repayment plan, usually three to five years. You keep your property, pay what the plan says, and eligible debt left over is discharged at the end.

slides.heading: How long it stays on a credit report
slides.note: Scores usually drop sharply at first and can recover with new on-time history.

slides.heading: What survives either one
items: Child support and alimony
Most student loans
Recent taxes and court fines
Secured loans, if you keep the collateral and stop paying

posts.caption:
Bankruptcy is not one thing. ⚖️ Chapter 7 discharges most unsecured debt in months but may involve selling non-exempt assets and has an income test. Chapter 13 is a 3-to-5-year repayment plan that lets you keep your property. Both stay on your credit report for years, and some debts survive either one. This is information, not legal advice. A bankruptcy attorney consultation is often free. Swipe ➡️

posts.title: Avalanche pays the highest rate first. Snowball pays the smallest balance first.

cover.title: Avalanche pays the highest rate first. Snowball pays the smallest balance first.
cover.subtitle: Which one wins? The one you keep doing.

slides.heading: The setup is the same
items: List every unsecured balance with its APR
Pay the minimum on all of them
Send every extra dollar to one target
When it is gone, roll that payment to the next

slides.heading: Avalanche: highest APR first
slides.body: Targets the most expensive debt. Over the whole payoff it costs the least in interest and finishes soonest on paper.

slides.heading: Snowball: smallest balance first
slides.body: Targets the account you can close fastest. Costs a bit more in interest, but every closed account is a visible win, and wins keep people going.

slides.heading: A hybrid that works
slides.body: Close one or two tiny balances first for momentum, then switch to highest rate. The cost difference is usually small. The consistency is what matters.

posts.caption:
Avalanche or snowball? The right answer is the one you will actually keep doing. ❄️🏔️ Avalanche: highest APR first, least interest paid. Snowball: smallest balance first, fastest visible wins. Either one beats spreading extra money thinly across every card. Swipe for the setup ➡️

posts.title: When an account goes to collections, the rules change.

cover.title: When an account goes to collections, the rules change.
cover.subtitle: Knowing the sequence takes the fear out of the phone.

slides.heading: Charge-off comes first
slides.body: After roughly six months without payment, the issuer charges the account off. That is an accounting step, not forgiveness. The debt is often sold or assigned to a collector.

slides.heading: Your rights on the first call
items: A written validation notice within five days of first contact
The amount, the original creditor, and how to dispute
You can ask for everything in writing before saying more

slides.heading: How long it can stay on your report
slides.label: from the original missed payment
slides.body: Whether or not it is later paid. Paid collections usually hurt less under newer scoring models.

slides.heading: Statutes of limitations
slides.body: Each state limits how long a collector can sue, commonly three to six years. The debt does not vanish, but a lawsuit gets much harder. In some states a small payment restarts the clock.

posts.caption:
A collector calling is not an emergency. Here is what actually happens at that stage. 📞 Charge-off after about six months. A written validation notice you can ask for. Seven years on your credit report from the first missed payment. A statute of limitations on lawsuits, usually three to six years depending on your state. Not legal advice, but knowing the sequence changes everything. Swipe ➡️

posts.title: Credit utilization is the fastest lever on your score.

cover.title: Credit utilization is the fastest lever on your score.
cover.subtitle: It has no memory. Change it and the score reacts next month.

slides.heading: What it is
slides.label: = $3,000 owed on a $10,000 limit
slides.body: Balance divided by limit. Scoring models look at each card and at all cards combined.

slides.heading: Why it counts so much
slides.body: Amounts owed are roughly a third of a FICO score, and utilization is most of that. High utilization signals strain even when every payment is on time.

slides.heading: The common guidance
items: Under 30% is the usual rule of thumb
Under 10% scores better still
One maxed-out card can drag the score even if the overall ratio is fine

slides.heading: The trap
slides.body: Closing a paid-off card removes its limit from the total and can raise your utilization overnight. Keeping old accounts open, at zero, usually helps.

posts.caption:
Credit utilization is the fastest lever on your score. 📈 Balance divided by limit, per card and overall. Under 30% is the usual rule; under 10% is better. It has no memory: lower the reported balance and the score reacts next cycle. One trap: closing a paid-off card can raise your utilization. Swipe to see why ➡️

posts.title: Consolidation, counseling, and settlement are three different tools.

cover.title: Consolidation, counseling, and settlement are three different tools.
cover.subtitle: Each fits a different situation. Here is how to tell.

slides.heading: Debt consolidation
slides.body: A new loan pays off several balances, leaving one payment, ideally at a lower rate. It needs decent credit to qualify, and it does not reduce what is owed.

slides.heading: Credit counseling plan
slides.body: A nonprofit agency sets up one monthly payment, and creditors often lower interest rates. The full balance is repaid over three to five years. Accounts are typically closed.

slides.heading: Debt settlement
slides.body: A company negotiates with creditors to accept less than the balance, paid from money set aside over time. It can affect credit scores, and forgiven amounts may be taxable.

slides.heading: Which fits when
items: Good credit and steady income: consolidation
Can repay in full over time: counseling
Cannot repay in full: settlement or a bankruptcy consultation
Not sure: an honest review should say

posts.caption:
Consolidation, credit counseling, and settlement are three different tools. 🧰 Consolidation: one new loan, needs good credit, same total owed. Counseling plan: one payment, often lower rates, everything repaid over a few years. Settlement: creditors accept less than the balance. It can affect credit scores and is not right for everyone. An honest review tells you which one fits, or if none do. Swipe ➡️

posts.title: Medical bills deserve a different first move than a credit card.

cover.title: Medical bills deserve a different first move than a credit card.
cover.subtitle: Four things to do before paying a dollar.

slides.heading: Before you pay
items: Ask for an itemized bill and check it against the insurer's statement
Ask the hospital about financial assistance
Ask for an interest-free payment plan
Ask all three before the account ages

slides.heading: Financial assistance is real
slides.body: Nonprofit hospitals are required to have financial assistance policies, and many reduce or waive bills below certain income levels. It has to be asked for. It is rarely offered.

slides.heading: Credit reporting is gentler now
items: Paid medical collections are no longer reported
Unpaid ones under $500 are not shown
Larger ones get a one-year wait before appearing
Rules keep shifting, so check your reports

slides.heading: Once it reaches collections
slides.body: A medical bill behaves like any other unsecured account. It can be part of a counseling plan or a settlement review, just like a card balance.

posts.caption:
Medical bills deserve a different first move than a credit card. 🏥 Ask for an itemized bill. Ask about financial assistance (nonprofit hospitals must have it). Ask for an interest-free payment plan before it ages. Credit reporting on medical debt is gentler than it used to be, but the rules keep changing. Swipe for the checklist ➡️

slides.body: Early payments mostly cover interest. Anything above that goes straight to principal, and a smaller principal charges less interest next month. Extra money compounds in your favor.

slides.heading: Where $50 usually hides
items: One unused subscription
One insurance quote
One phone plan review
Then set autopay to the new amount, once

posts.caption:

posts.title: Your card issuer has a hardship program. They will not call to tell you.

cover.title: Your card issuer has a hardship program. They will not call to tell you.
cover.subtitle: Here is how to ask for it.

slides.heading: What it is
slides.body: A temporary arrangement from the issuer itself: a lower APR for a set period, waived late fees, or a fixed monthly payment. Built for job loss, illness, or an income drop.

slides.heading: How to ask
items: Call the number on the back of the card
Ask for the hardship or financial assistance department
Explain the situation in one or two sentences
Ask what programs exist, then get the terms in writing

slides.heading: What to expect
slides.body: Often six to twelve months of reduced interest or a fixed payment. The card is usually frozen or closed for new purchases while the program runs.

slides.heading: Where it fits
slides.body: Best for a temporary setback with a clear end. For balances that cannot be repaid in full even at a lower rate, a counseling plan or settlement review may fit better.

posts.caption:
Your card issuer probably has a hardship program. They will not call to tell you about it. ☎️ Lower APR for a set period, waived fees, or a fixed payment, usually for job loss, illness, or an income drop. You ask for the hardship department; you get the terms in writing. It fits a temporary problem with an end date. Swipe for how to ask ➡️

cover.title: Five questions to ask before agreeing to any debt plan.
cover.subtitle: Including with us.

slides.heading: Ask about money
items: What is the total cost, in dollars, for the whole plan?
When exactly are fees charged?

slides.heading: Ask about consequences
items: What happens to my credit scores?
What happens if I miss a payment?

slides.heading: Ask about them
items: Are you licensed or registered in my state?
Can I have all of this in writing?

slides.heading: What a good answer sounds like
slides.body: Specific. In dollars, not percentages. Honest about credit. Clear on fees. Vague answers to any of these are your cue to keep looking.

posts.caption:
